stories.topic: Five Biryanis Within Five Kilometres of Mangalore
stories.summary: Amit and about fifteen friends went on a food trip through Mysore and Mangalore by bus. They planned their stops on an Excel sheet and ate around eight meals a day. In one area within roughly five kilometres of Mangalore, they found five different kinds of biryani. Each had arisen in its own way, and each was authentic to the place.
stories.insight: Globalisation shows up on a single street, not only in abstract trade statistics. What we call 'authentic' local food is the layered result of exchange, which is why Amit thinks the cultural case for trade may be the strongest one of all.
stories.quote: there is one area, I think, within a five kilometer radius of Mangalore, where you get five different kinds of biryani, and they're all authentic to the place.

stories.topic: Islam First Came to India Through Trade, Not Conquest
stories.summary: Most people assume Islam arrived in India with invaders a few hundred years ago. Amit points out that well before that, during the Prophet Muhammad's own lifetime, Muslims came to the south of India, to Kerala as he recalls it, as traders. He uses this to show that trade routes carry religions and ideas along with goods.
stories.insight: The popular story of how a faith arrived can hide an older and gentler one. Trade has always carried ideas, and most cultural mixing has happened through voluntary exchange rather than force.
stories.quote: But before that, during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad himself, Muslims came to India as traders to the south.

stories.topic: How India Missed the Bus That the East Asian Tigers Caught
stories.summary: Around 1950, India was doing well next to South Korea and Taiwan. It had democracy and many other advantages. India kept its markets closed, while the East Asian Tigers opened theirs, reached economies of scale, raised their standards by competing globally, and took off. Through the 1960s and 70s, India could have used its cheap labour to build mass manufacturing. Terrible labour and industrial laws held it back. Bangladesh is winning today because it embraced that path. India later found a niche in services mostly because many of its people were educated in English.
stories.insight: Comparative advantage only pays off if policy lets you use it. Starting with more advantages counts for little if you shut the door that lets you scale them.
stories.quote: we should have been the ones who succeeded, who had embraced democracy, who had so many good things going for them. But we kept our markets closed

stories.topic: The Rent-Seeking Entrepreneurs of Amit's Youth
stories.summary: Jagdish Bhagwati once observed that people's mentality in China is profit-seeking while in India it is rent-seeking. Amit says he and a former colleague of Ajay's once planned to write a piece on this. In his younger years, Amit was often shocked that people who wanted to start a business thought in exploitative terms. Their plan was to get rich through the state, either by becoming part of it or by becoming its crony, using tariffs on competitors or entry barriers.
stories.insight: A closed economy does more than slow growth. It shapes how a whole generation thinks about making money. When the path to prosperity runs through the state, ambitious people learn to capture the state instead of serving customers.
stories.quote: in all my young years, whenever I'd meet someone who wanted to start a business, I was often shocked

stories.topic: It Wasn't the Crash. It Was the Tariffs.
stories.summary: Popular memory dates the Great Depression to the October 1929 stock market crash. Drawing on Thomas Sowell, Amit tells it differently. Unemployment peaked at 9% a couple of months after the crash and then fell to 6.3% by June 1930. President Hoover then tried to lift employment by protecting domestic manufacturers with the Smoot-Hawley tariffs. Other countries retaliated and a trade war followed. Within five months US unemployment was back above 10%, and it stayed in double digits for the rest of the 1930s. Sowell, now 94, recently gave an interview saying Trump's tariffs are the same thing happening again.
stories.insight: The policy response, not the original shock, turned a downturn into a decade-long catastrophe. The tariff logic of the 1930s is the same zero-sum logic driving tariff talk today.
stories.quote: Within five months, the unemployment shoots back up to over ten percent, and for the rest of the nineteen thirties, it is a double digit figure.

stories.topic: The Line From Smoot-Hawley to the Second World War
stories.summary: Ajay recalls that global trade fell by about 66% after Smoot-Hawley. He traces two routes from there to war. First, economic hardship hollows out the political centre and boosts extremists, whether national socialist or communist. Second, if you cannot buy what you need, such as rare earths from Africa, you start thinking about marching in and taking it. After 1930 came the Japanese invasion of 1931, Italy's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935, and Germany's push for Lebensraum. Mein Kampf predates the tariffs, but Smoot-Hawley strengthened the German belief that the global trading system was British-controlled, especially after the British blockade in World War I, and that Germany must conquer land to prosper.
stories.insight: Trade is more than a route to prosperity. It is the peaceful alternative to taking things by force. Shut down voluntary exchange and you push nations back toward conquest.
stories.quote: there are lines that run from Smoot-Hawley all the way to the second world war.

stories.topic: The 1909 Book That Declared War Impossible
stories.summary: The first wave of globalisation in the 19th century, built on the ideas of Smith and Ricardo, felt so settled that Norman Angell argued in The Great Illusion (1909) that war was now impossible because nations were too intertwined by trade. The next decade brought World War I. Keynes later described the lost world in The Economic Consequences of the Peace: in 1914 a Londoner could order goods from across the earth by telephone over his morning tea. The war left people cynical and led to disastrous decades that followed.
stories.insight: Being right about the benefits of trade is not the same as those benefits being secure. Amit admits that he and Ajay also 'drank the Kool-Aid' of believing the globalised order was a done deal.
stories.quote: some people drunk the Kool-Aid, like even you and I have drunk the Kool Aid, not in terms of the value of these ideas or the benefits of free trade, but in believing that it was now a done deal.

recommendations.reason: A fantastic book for learning the basic concepts in simple language. Amit calls Sowell a towering thinker of the 20th century and says you should read all his books.

recommendations.context: Part of the closing reading list for this economics 101 episode.
recommendations.reason: One of Amit's core picks for building first-principles economic intuition.

recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Amit recommends 'everything by Frédéric Bastiat' in the closing list. The show notes link this collection.

recommendations.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
recommendations.context: Ajay's pick when Amit hands over to him at the end: 'The globalization book by Jagdish Bhagwati. That's the one.'
recommendations.reason: His single go-to book on the subject. Bhagwati's work also underlies the episode's elite-conflict and rent-seeking arguments.

recommendations.item: The Wealth of Nations
recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Comes up while tracing how ideas defeated mercantilism.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says Smith is to economics what Darwin is to biology. The first grand ideas and deep intuitions of economics are all here, and it is 'eerie' how much Smith got right.

recommendations.item: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Amit adds it right after Ajay praises The Wealth of Nations.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Smith's earlier book a philosophical masterpiece in its own right.

recommendations.item: Conversation and Society (Episode 182, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Russ Roberts
recommendations.context: Amit mentions he has an episode on The Theory of Moral Sentiments with Russ Roberts.
recommendations.reason: A way into Smith's moral philosophy for anyone who wants more than his economics.

recommendations.item: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
recommendations.creator: John Maynard Keynes
recommendations.context: Amit calls it Keynes's 'great book' and reads its famous passage about the 1914 Londoner ordering the world's goods over morning tea.
recommendations.reason: A vivid record of how globalised the pre-WWI world was, and of what war destroyed.

recommendations.item: The Great Illusion
recommendations.creator: Norman Angell
recommendations.context: Cited as the 1909 book arguing that trade had made war impossible, a decade before World War I.
recommendations.reason: Worth knowing as a cautionary tale. Trade's incentives are real, but treating them as a guarantee is a mistake.

recommendations.item: Thomas Sowell interviewed by Peter Robinson
recommendations.creator: Peter Robinson with Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Amit notes that Sowell, now 94, recently gave an interview about Trump's tariffs.
recommendations.reason: Sowell, who wrote about Smoot-Hawley decades ago, says today's tariffs are the same thing happening again.

recommendations.item: I, Pencil
recommendations.creator: Leonard Read
recommendations.context: Amit's 'great essay we keep talking about on this show', cited while explaining hyper-specialisation.
recommendations.reason: Told in the first person by a pencil, it shows how people in many countries cooperate to make a simple product, coordinated only by prices and not by any central planner.

recommendations.item: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Source of the phrase Amit uses to explain why voluntary trade benefits both sides.
recommendations.reason: Amit loves the phrase as the simplest picture of positive-sum exchange: you thank the barista for the coffee and the barista thanks you for the money.

recommendations.item: A trade deficit with a babysitter
recommendations.creator: Tim Harford
recommendations.context: Amit's 'great essay I've referred to a few times on the show', used to bust the trade-deficit myth.
recommendations.reason: Harford runs a permanent trade deficit with his babysitter and both are better off, which shows why the word 'deficit' misleads.

recommendations.item: A brief history of globalization
recommendations.creator: Peter Vanham
recommendations.context: Amit reads from this World Economic Forum piece about the Columbian Exchange.
recommendations.reason: A concise overview of how trade reshaped what the world eats: imagine Italian cuisine without tomatoes, or Irish history without the potato.

recommendations.reason: The longer version of his argument that in a positive-sum world, inequality can rise while poverty falls, as happened in India after 1991.

core_ideas.concept: The Freedom Argument: Who Is the State to Stop a Voluntary Exchange?
core_ideas.explanation: The first reason trade is good is moral, not economic. If two people want to trade voluntarily and no one else's rights are infringed, nobody has any business stopping them, and it shouldn't matter whether one is in India and the other in Washington, DC. Amit notes that ideologies are inconsistent here: some defend freedom in the bedroom but not the marketplace, others the reverse. Ajay says calling Pune or Mozambique to make a deal is the same act, and this point should be made first.
core_ideas.quote: if you and I want to associate with each other in any way that is voluntary, who is anybody else to stop us?

core_ideas.concept: Trade Is Positive-Sum: The Double Thank You Moment
core_ideas.explanation: When you buy coffee, you value the coffee more than the money and the seller values the money more than the coffee, so both say thank you. Tennis is zero-sum, but voluntary exchange is not, whether between individuals, firms or countries. The key word is voluntary, so colonial extraction does not count as free trade. Every trade that is blocked destroys value that would otherwise have existed.
core_ideas.quote: every voluntary action between two consenting adults is always a positive sum game. It is a double thank you moment.

core_ideas.concept: Comparative Advantage: Ratios, Not Being the Best
core_ideas.explanation: David Ricardo's example: even if Portugal is better than England at making both cloth and wine, both countries end up with more of each if each specialises and trades. Amit's version: even if Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma were the best drivers in Bombay, they should hire a chauffeur and spend their minds on cricket and acting. Ajay's takeaway for India is that being poor or not world-class at anything is no barrier to gaining from trade, because what matters is the ratio of relative superiority.
core_ideas.quote: imagine I'm bad at many, many things. We will still be better off trading because the ratio of how much you are superior to me will vary.

core_ideas.explanation: Imagine growing, cooking and cleaning everything for yourself. Anyone who truly tries to be self-sufficient is instantly poor. We prosper by specialising and buying everything else: Amit podcasts and buys his cauliflower. The same applies to nations, so 'our country should make everything' rhetoric gets prosperity backwards. A country's advantage often comes from its endowments, such as cheap labour or an English-educated workforce.
core_ideas.quote: The more you specialize, the richer you will get, and the more you can actually get all the goodies of life.

core_ideas.explanation: A market of ten shirt buyers doesn't justify a machine. A global market justifies investment that raises quality and lowers cost. A phone can be designed in Silicon Valley, use African rare earths, Taiwanese chips and Chinese assembly, much like Leonard Read's pencil, coordinated only by prices. The world effectively outsources aircraft to two competitors, Boeing and Airbus. Ajay adds the firm's view: you max out in one country, and the world is the next ladder, which is why the biggest corporations are multinationals.
core_ideas.quote: If each country had to make its own aircraft, then imagine what would happen.

core_ideas.concept: Growth Is Contagious, and Poverty Is Not Inequality
core_ideas.explanation: In a globalised world, one country's rising middle class becomes another's export market: China buys German machines and Australian minerals. A World Bank study found free trade cut poverty and reduced global inequality. Global extreme poverty fell from 35% to 10% between 1988 and 2013. Within India after 1991, inequality rose but poverty fell. Amit's test question: would you rather be poor in Bangladesh or the USA? People pick the USA, which has more inequality but less poverty.
core_ideas.quote: it's a positive sum world where everybody can get richer at different rates. And therefore inequality and poverty are very different things.

core_ideas.concept: Economic Growth Is the Whole Game
core_ideas.explanation: Lant Pritchett's paper, discussed in an earlier episode, shows that per capita GDP is the key factor behind every human welfare indicator, from health onwards. Amit puts it as roughly 99% versus 1% for welfare redistribution. Their friend Nitin Pai estimated that each 1% of GDP growth lifts a million people out of poverty, a figure he later revised to two million. For Amit this makes growth a moral matter, not something for elites to debate abstractly.
core_ideas.quote: Economics is not a dry subject to do with numbers. It has moral and human consequence

core_ideas.explanation: Nothing we treasure as 'ours' is purely home-grown. The Silk Road carried religions and ideas along with goods. The Columbian Exchange brought India the potato, the chilli and the guava. Stitched clothing came from outside. Globalisation is the source of culture, not a threat to it. Ajay's alternative picture is a shallow North Korea behind a high wall.
core_ideas.quote: No culture is something sui generis. Every culture is a khichri.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay builds on Bhagwati, Srinivasan and Krueger. In a closed economy, elites see a fixed pie and fight wastefully over slices, which raises conflict in the country. Once the arena becomes the world market, elites find common ground in policies that make the country strong and competitive, so conflict falls and better policy gets done.
core_ideas.quote: when you close the economy, then the domestic elites see the economy as a finite landscape and they start fighting with each other to grab a slice of the pie.

core_ideas.explanation: Profit-seeking means making money by giving others value in a double-thank-you exchange. Rent-seeking means extracting money, for example through state monopolies, cronyism, tariffs on competitors or entry barriers. Bhagwati saw China as profit-seeking and India as rent-seeking. Amit argues that decades of a closed economy produced this, because the levers of prosperity sat with the state.
core_ideas.quote: if you are open, then you are competing in the global marketplace and you'll have a profit seeking mentality. But if you are closed, then you and I are fighting for a fixed pie and then it is dog-eat-dog.

core_ideas.concept: Mercantilism vs 'The Real Fun Is in Importing'
core_ideas.explanation: From the 16th to the 18th century, kings saw trade as zero-sum: exports bring in gold, imports send it out, so aim for a surplus. Alexander Hamilton's 'infant industry' tariffs came from the same thinking, and Trump's balance-sheet view of trade echoes it. Smith and Ricardo flipped the frame. We export only to earn the means to import the world's goods. Ajay's 1,100-rupee Casio watch exists only because he can buy from overseas. The export obsession serves governments, not citizens.
core_ideas.quote: There's no fun in exporting. The real fun is in importing.

core_ideas.concept: Trade Is the Peaceful Alternative to War
core_ideas.explanation: War is negative-sum and trade is positive-sum. When trade breaks down, two things follow. Hardship erodes the political centre and feeds extremists, and nations that cannot buy what they need start thinking about seizing it. Ajay's rare-earths example: if trade fails, someone decides to 'bloody march into Africa' and take them. Defending trade also means defending peace.
core_ideas.quote: it is very important to see trade not just as a lovely way to harness comparative advantage and prosperity, but also to stop the madness of nationalism and war

core_ideas.concept: Your Own Consumers Pay the Tariff, Twice
core_ideas.explanation: A 100-rupee import with a 10% tariff sells for 110, and the domestic buyer pays the difference, not the foreign exporter. It goes further: if a 500-rupee foreign shirt becomes 550, Indian shirt-makers raise their prices to 550 as well. Consumers pay more for foreign and domestic goods alike.
core_ideas.quote: So consumers pay for the tariff. There is just no way around that.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's half-joking law: every interference in free markets moves wealth from the poor to the rich. Suppose a Chinese widget costs 100 rupees and the Indian one 110. A 20-rupee tariff forces buyers onto the 110-rupee local version. That extra 10 rupees, taken from many consumers, would otherwise have funded other double-thank-you transactions and jobs. Instead it goes to one protected interest group. Tariffs are always a tax on your own poor.
core_ideas.quote: every interference in free markets redistributes wealth from the poor to the rich. And tariffs are an indisputable example of this.

core_ideas.explanation: Since a tariff taxes your own citizens, 'retaliating' against another country's tariffs just hurts your own people a second time. Joan Robinson put it this way: other countries putting rocks in their harbours is no reason to put rocks in ours. Amit's position is that India should cut tariffs to zero on everything, whatever others do.
core_ideas.quote: A tariff is an attack on your own people.

core_ideas.concept: A Trade Deficit Is Accounting, Not a Loss
core_ideas.explanation: In any market, the quantity bought equals the quantity sold after the fact. That holds for tomatoes and it holds for dollars. Capital flows (foreigners buying Indian shares, Indians buying London homes) and trade flows (importing microphones or Diet Coke) must sum to zero. An investment boom that brings capital in therefore requires a trade deficit. Amit adds that individuals trade, not countries, and Tim Harford runs a happy permanent deficit with his babysitter. Saying 'we made a loss trading with China' is a basic failure of economics.
core_ideas.quote: It's an accounting fact that if you have capital coming into a country, you will always have a deficit on the trade account.

core_ideas.concept: Tariffs Hurt the Industries They Claim to Protect
core_ideas.explanation: Around half of US imports are inputs that local manufacturers use, so tariffs make domestic products more expensive too. Sheltered firms compete for influence with the government instead of competing to serve customers, and they stagnate. Ajay's example is decades of the Ambassador and the Premier Padmini behind trade barriers, which did not produce a great Indian car industry.
core_ideas.quote: a company that has to compete with global competitors will, you know, import best practices, lift its standards, do better.

core_ideas.explanation: Many people have an 'almost mystical attachment' to goods and manufacturing because you can touch a car. Trade figures often leave out services, and the current account is the right measure. Before fibre-optic cables, services couldn't be traded. Today they can, so barriers should go both ways: global law firms should be able to operate in India and Indian firms abroad. Growth is about productivity, whatever form the output takes.
core_ideas.quote: there is no reason to think that a ball bearing is somehow better or superior than a call center call.

core_ideas.concept: 1991–2011: India's Best Era Was an Openness Story, Not a Party Story
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls the fourfold GDP gain from 1991 to 2011 India's greatest economic achievement, and links it causally to trade barriers and capital controls steadily falling from 1991 to 2008. Amit stresses that this cuts across parties. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh began it, the Vajpayee government advanced it, and later governments of both parties got many things wrong. He also says the import-substitution thinking of the Nehru era and today's self-reliance rhetoric share the same bad economics.
core_ideas.quote: The greatest ever economic achievement of India in the last 10,000 years was the 4x gain of GDP that happened from 1991 to 2011.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit takes over the comparative-advantage example from Ajay ('Let me break this down because you will find a way to mess it up'), then asks us to assume Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma are the best drivers in Bombay: 'Actually they're not. I am.'
Amit on camera craft: 'You should look at the camera and say, Amit said, or you should look at me and say as you said, which would suitably flatter me that I'm being quoted to myself.'
Amit: 'bookmark this episode, but watch it now. Don't bookmark it and never watch it... Ajay, you do that a lot, don't you? You've bookmarked Perfect Days.'
Ajay on the claim that exporters pay tariffs: 'I've never heard this idea in my whole life until one low IQ American president said it.'
Amit acting out the local manufacturer asking for protection: 'See, I'm crying, I'm an infant, protect me.'
After Ajay argues goods and services are equal, Amit worries Trump might conclude: 'Why should I put tariffs only on goods? I will also put tariffs on services. And it will be your fault, Ajay.'

Amit on India's protectionism: what Nehru-ji did and Modi-ji is doing are much the same, 'like one is a successor of the other in terms of bad economic thinking. In other ways they are very, very, very different.'

Amit's jab at critics of growth: 'It is okay for elites to sit in their air conditioned rooms sipping their single malt to talk about neoliberal values', while growth is what puts food on people's plates.
On the post-war economics consensus: 'left ho ya, right ho ya, center ho ya, kuch bhi ho', meaning whether left, right, centre or anything else, economists agreed globalisation was good.
The Economist was founded in 1843 to defend free trade and, as Amit notes, 'still calls itself a newspaper, by the way, for some reason.'
Joan Robinson: just because other countries put rocks in their harbour doesn't mean we have to put rocks in ours. Amit uses it to dismiss 'reciprocal' tariffs.
Ajay applies 'An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind' to tit-for-tat trade wars.
Ajay: 'Adam Smith is to economics, what Charles Darwin is to biology.' Amit, who doesn't believe in the great man theory of history, makes an exception for Smith.
Richard Cobden's campaign that got the Corn Laws repealed in 1846, and Pax Britannica's control of the seas, are cited as 19th-century milestones for free trade.

Counter-currents to free trade: Alexander Hamilton, the mercantilist who popularised 'infant industry' protection (against Jefferson, 'more of a freedom guy'), and Friedrich List's German economic nationalism.
Marx and Engels, in Amit's view, got the description right and the analysis wrong: 'national one-sidedness and narrow-mindedness become more and more impossible.'
Lebensraum: Ajay links Germany's conquest-for-resources ideology, and its sense of a British-controlled trading system after the WWI blockade, to the collapse of trade after Smoot-Hawley.
From Peter Vanham's WEF piece on the Columbian Exchange: 'Imagine Italian cuisine without tomatoes, which came from the new world, or Irish history without the potato.'

The Washington Consensus (named in 1989): the late-20th-century agreement on globalisation, left for the next episode, along with industrial-country tariffs falling from about 40% to under 5% after 1945.

Ajay frames his life as a series of crises he was fully absorbed in: the 1997 East Asian crisis, 9/11, 2008 and the pandemic. He calls today's mix of populism, trade and geopolitics another such moment.
